narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 56% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. By far the strongest factor was your third-year class ranking, which placed you in the bottom decile of your school. This was the most influential piece of information and strongly pushed the model toward predicting failure. Your first-year ranking in the fourth decile also mattered, but in the opposite direction: it provided a modest pull toward success. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.4, noticeably below the 3.23 average of accepted students, added a further push toward predicting that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Taken together, these academic signals outweighed other details such as your LSAT score of 30, your upper-middle family income, your part-time enrollment plans, and your demographic background, none of which played a meaningful role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic foundation. Consider retaking key courses to raise your GPA, seeking structured bar-prep support early, or gaining additional legal experience that demonstrates your ability to handle rigorous material. Reapplying with a stronger academic record will give the model a very different picture of your likelihood of passing the bar. (218 words)
